By Mount Sinai (al-Tur), and by a Book inscribed, on unrolled parchment, and by the House frequented, and by the raised canopy, and by the sea kindled. Indeed, the punishment of your Lord will surely occur; none can avert it.

Qur'anic verse: ﴿By Mount Sinai (al-Tur)﴾. Al-Tur is the name of the mountain on which Allah spoke to Musa. Allah swore by it to honour it, to ennoble it, and to remind of the signs that are in it. It is one of the mountains of Paradise. Isma'il ibn Ishaq narrated, saying: Isma'il ibn Abi Uways narrated to us, saying: Kathir ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn 'Awf narrated to us from his father, from his grandfather, that he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Four mountains are from the mountains of Paradise, and four rivers are from the rivers of Paradise, and four battles (malahim) are from the battles of Paradise." [[al-Malahim: the battles of Badr, Uhud, al-Khandaq and Khaybar.]] It was said: "What are the four mountains?" He said: "Mount Uhud, which loves us and we love it; and al-Tur is a mountain of the mountains of Paradise; and Lubnan is a mountain of the mountains of Paradise; [and al-Judi [[The addition is from n.]] is a mountain of the mountains of Paradise]." (He mentioned the hadith, and we have fully covered it in the book al-Tadhkira.)

Mujahid said: al-Tur in Syriac means "the mountain," and what is meant by it is Tur Sina (Sinai). Al-Suddi also said this. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: there are two Turs; one is called Tur Sina and the other Tur Zayta, because they grow figs and olives. It was also said: it is a mountain in Madyan, named Zubayr. Al-Jawhari said: al-Zubayr is the mountain on which Allah spoke to Musa, peace be upon him.

I say: Madyan is in the Holy Land, and it is the town of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. It was also said: al-Tur is every mountain that grows plants, and whatever does not grow plants is not a tur; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. This has been discussed in full in al-Baqara [[See vol. 1, p. 436.]].

Allah's words: ﴿and by a Book inscribed﴾, that is, written. It means the Qur'an, which the believers read from the mushafs and which the angels read from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), as Allah says: "Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an, in a Book well-guarded" [[See pp. 224 and 308 of this part.]]. It was also said: it means the other revealed books sent down to the prophets, and every book was on parchment which its people unrolled to read. Al-Kalbi said: it is what Allah wrote for Musa with His own hand from the Torah, while Musa heard the scratching of the pen. Al-Farra' said: it means the records of deeds: some take their book in the right hand and some take their book in the left; compare: "And We will bring forth for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find spread open" [[See vol. 10, p. 229.]], and His saying: "And when the pages are unfolded" [[See vol. 19, p. 232.]]. It was also said: it is the Book which Allah wrote for His angels in the heavens, in which they read what has been and what will be. It was also said: what is meant is what Allah wrote in the hearts of the righteous believers; its proof is: "Those, He has written faith in their hearts" [[See pp. 224 and 308 of this part.]]. I say: in this view there is a figurative usage, since it expresses the parchment by the hearts. Al-Mubarrad said: al-raqq is the skin that has been thinned so that one may write on it, and al-manshur is the spread-out. Al-Jawhari also said so in al-Sihah, and he said: al-raqq (with a fatha) is what is written upon, and it is a thin skin. From this is Allah's saying: ﴿on unrolled parchment﴾. Al-raqq also means a large tortoise. Abu 'Ubayda said: its plural is ruquq. The intended meaning is what al-Farra' said, and Allah knows best. Every page is called raqq because of the thinness of its edges, and from this is the saying of al-Mutalammis:

"As if it were, from the age of its tradition, a parchment whose book is written out [[I have not found this verse in the Diwan of al-Mutalammis.]]"

As for al-riqq (with a kasra), it means ownership; one says: a slave who is owned (ma'ruq). Al-Mawardi related from Ibn 'Abbas that al-raqq (with a fatha) is what lies between the East and the West.

Allah's words: ﴿and by the House frequented﴾. 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and others said: it is a house in the heavens, directly opposite the Ka'ba, which seventy thousand angels enter every day; then they leave and do not return to it. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is a house in the sixth heaven. It was also said: in the fourth heaven. Anas ibn Malik narrated from Malik ibn Sa'sa'a, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I was brought up to the fourth heaven, and the House frequented (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur) was raised for us, and behold, it was directly opposite the Ka'ba; if it were to fall, it would fall upon it. Seventy thousand angels enter it every day, and when they leave it they do not return to it." Al-Mawardi mentioned it. Al-Qushayri related from Ibn 'Abbas that it is in the lowest heaven. Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: Ibn al-Kawwa' asked 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "What is the House frequented?" He said: "A house above seven heavens, beneath the Throne, called al-Durah." Likewise in al-Sihah: al-Durah (with a damma) is a house in the heaven, and it is the House frequented, from Ibn 'Abbas. And its being frequented is due to the abundance of its visiting angels. Al-Mahdawi related from him: opposite the Throne. What is in Sahih Muslim from Malik ibn Sa'sa'a, from the Prophet ﷺ, in the hadith of the Night Journey: "Then I was raised to the House frequented, and I said: 'O Jibril, what is this?' He said: 'This is the House frequented; seventy thousand angels enter it every day, and when they leave they do not return to it, [the last of them] (akhir ma 'alayhim)." [[(akhir) with a raised or a fatha on the ra'; the fatha is adverbial, and the raising is on the assumption of "that is the last of what is upon them"; the raising is more preferable. (Marginal note on Muslim).]] He then mentioned the hadith. In the hadith of Thabit from Anas ibn Malik, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I was brought the Buraq," the hadith, and in it: "Then we ascended to the seventh [heaven]" [[In ḥ, z, l, n: "to the seventh heaven."]], "and Jibril asked for opening, and it was said: 'Who is this?' He said: 'Jibril.' It was said: 'And who is with you?' He said: 'Muhammad ﷺ.' It was said: 'And has he been sent for?' He said: 'He has been sent for.' So it was opened for us, and behold, I found Ibrahim, peace be upon him, leaning his back against the House frequented, and it is entered every day by seventy thousand angels who do not return to it." Also from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: For Allah in the heavens and the earths there are fifteen houses: seven in the heavens, seven in the earths, and the Ka'ba; and all of them are opposite the Ka'ba. Al-Hasan said: the House frequented is the Ka'ba, the Sacred House which is frequented by people; Allah sustains it each year with six hundred thousand [visitors]; if people are unable to do that, Allah completes it with the angels; and it is the first house which Allah set up for worship on the earth. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: the House frequented was on the earth at the place of the Ka'ba in the time of Adam, peace be upon him; then in the time of Nuh, peace be upon him, he commanded them to make pilgrimage, but they refused and disobeyed him. When the water rose, it was lifted and placed opposite it in the lowest heaven, where seventy thousand angels frequent it every day, and then they do not return to it until the Trumpet is blown. He said: Then Allah, mighty and majestic, settled Ibrahim in the place of the House where it had been. Allah said: "And when We settled for Ibrahim the place of the House, [saying]: Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circumambulate, stand, bow and prostrate" [[See vol. 13, p. (36).]], and ﴿the raised canopy﴾: it means the heaven, which He called a canopy because for the earth it is like a canopy for the house. Its proof is: "And We made the heaven a protected canopy" [[See vol. 11, p. (285).]]. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the Throne, and it is the ceiling of Paradise.

﴿And the sea kindled﴾. Mujahid said: "al-masjur" means kindled. A report has come: "The sea will be kindled on the Day of Resurrection and will become fire." Qatada said: it means filled. The grammarians cited the verse of al-Namir ibn Taulab:

"When it wishes, it looks upon a filled [spring]; around it you see the nab' and the sasam [[al-sasam, without hamz, is a tree from which bows and arrows are made, and the nab' is similar.]]"

He means a wild ass which looks at a spring that is filled (masjura). So it is permissible that the filled one is fire, which would be like the earlier saying. Likewise said al-Dahhak, Shimr ibn 'Atiyya, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and al-Akhfash: it is the kindled oven, heated, like the kindled tannur (oven). From this it is said that the bellows is misjar. The proof of this interpretation is Allah's saying: "And when the seas are set ablaze" [[See vol. 19, pp. 228 and 242.]], that is, kindled; I kindled the oven, sajartuhu sajran, meaning I heated it. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said to a Jewish man: "Where is Hell?" He said: "The sea." He said: "I see you are only telling the truth," and he recited: "and the sea kindled."

("And when the seas are set ablaze") is read with a light pronunciation. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr said: one should not perform wudu' with sea water, because it is the layer of Hell. [Ka'b said: The sea will be kindled tomorrow and added to the fire of Hell; this is one saying.]

Ibn 'Abbas said: al-masjur is the one whose water has gone. Abu al-'Aliya said the same. 'Atiyya and Dhu al-Rumma the poet related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: A slave-woman went out to draw water and said: "The basin is masjur," that is, empty. Ibn Abi Dawud said: Dhu al-Rumma has no narration except this. It was also said: al-masjur means al-mafjur (burst forth), its proof being: "And when the seas are burst forth" [[What is between the squares is missing from ha.]], that is, the earth dries them up so that no water remains in them.

A third view is that of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and 'Ikrima. Abu Makin said: I asked 'Ikrima about the sea that is masjur, and he said: it is a sea below the Throne. 'Ali said: beneath the Throne there is thick water, called the Sea of Life; people will be rained upon from it forty mornings after the first blast, and they will sprout in their graves. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: al-masjur is the one in which fresh and salt water are mixed. I say: and to this returns the meaning of "burst forth" in one of the two interpretations, that is, its fresh water bursts into its salt water; and Allah knows best. This will come. 'Ali ibn Abi Talha related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: al-masjur is the confined.

﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord will surely occur﴾: this is the answer to the oath, that is, it will befall the polytheists. Jubayr ibn Mut'im said: I came to Madina to ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the prisoners of Badr, and I found him reciting in the Maghrib prayer "al-Tur," up to His saying: "Indeed, the punishment of your Lord will surely occur; none can avert it." It was as if my heart was split, and I embraced Islam out of fear of the descent of the punishment, and I did not think I would rise from my place before the punishment befell me. Hisham ibn Hassan said: I went with Malik ibn Dinar to al-Hasan, and with him was a man reciting "al-Tur" until he reached "Indeed, the punishment of your Lord will surely occur; none can avert it." Al-Hasan wept, and his companions wept, and Malik began to tremble until he fainted. When Bakkar was appointed judge, two men came to him disputing, and the oath was incumbent upon one of them. He sought reconciliation between them, offering his opponent a compensation from his own wealth in place of the oath, but he refused except the oath. So [Bakkar] made him swear by the beginning of "al-Tur," until he said to him: "Say: 'Indeed, the punishment of your Lord will surely occur,' if you are lying." He said it, and went out, and was struck down at that very moment.

Anas ibn Malik narrated from Malik ibn Sa'sa'a, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I was brought up to the fourth heaven, and the House frequented (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur) was raised for us, and behold, it was directly opposite the Ka'ba; if it were to fall, it would fall upon it. He said: 'Jibril.' It was said: 'And who is with you?' He said: 'Muhammad ﷺ.' It was said: 'And has he been sent for?' He said: 'He has been sent for.' So it was opened for us, and behold, I found Ibrahim, peace be upon him, leaning his back against the House frequented, and it is entered every day by seventy thousand angels who do not return to it." Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: the House frequented was on the earth at the place of the Ka'ba in the time of Adam, peace be upon him; then in the time of Nuh, peace be upon him, he commanded them to make pilgrimage, but they refused and disobeyed him. When the water rose, it was lifted and placed opposite it in the lowest heaven, where seventy thousand angels frequent it every day, and then they do not return to it until the Trumpet is blown. He said: Then Allah, mighty and majestic, settled Ibrahim in the place of the House where it had been. (36).]], and ﴿the raised canopy﴾: it means the heaven, which He called a canopy because for the earth it is like a canopy for the house. ﴿And the sea kindled﴾. Mujahid said: "al-masjur" means kindled. A report has come: "The sea will be kindled on the Day of Resurrection and will become fire." Qatada said: it means filled. The grammarians cited the verse of al-Namir ibn Taulab:

"When it wishes, it looks upon a filled [spring]; around it you see the nab' and the sasam [[al-sasam, without hamz, is a tree from which bows and arrows are made, and the nab' is similar.]]"

He means a wild ass which looks at a spring that is filled (masjura). So it is permissible that the filled one is fire, which would be like the earlier saying. Likewise said al-Dahhak, Shimr ibn 'Atiyya, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and al-Akhfash: it is the kindled oven, heated, like the kindled tannur (oven). From this it is said that the bellows is misjar. ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord will surely occur﴾: this is the answer to the oath, that is, it will befall the polytheists. **Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 52, verses 9–16:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿On the Day when the sky will sway violently﴾. The word that governs "the Day" (yawm) in His saying "will surely occur" means: the punishment will befall them on the Day of Resurrection, and it is the Day on which the sky will sway. The people of lexicography (ahl al-lugha) said: "māra al-shay'u yamūru mawran" means it moved, came and went, as a tall date palm (al-nakhla al-ʿaydāna, i.e., the tall one) sways, and "al-tamawwur" is similar to it. Al-Dahhak said: some of it will surge into others. Mujahid said: it will revolve in a circular motion. Abu Ubayda and al-Akhfash said: it will tilt. He cited al-A'sha:

*As if her gait, from her neighbour's house,*
*Is the drifting of a cloud, neither slow nor hasty.*

It was also said: it will flow in a flowing manner. From this is the saying of Jarir:

*The slain kept their blood flowing in the Tigris,*
*until the water of the Tigris turned reddish-white.* [[al-ashkal: that in which there is whiteness and redness.]]

Ibn ʿAbbas said: on that Day the sky will sway with what is in it and will be agitated. It was also said: its people will revolve in it and some of them will surge into others. Al-mawr also means the road. From this is the saying of Tarafa:

*... over a well-trodden road.* [[The line is from his Mu'allaqa, and its full verse is:*
*They race against swift, noble she-camels, following*
*A sturdy leg over a well-trodden road.*
*Tabari: contending. Al-ʿitaq: noble she-camels. Al-nājiyāt: the swift ones. Al-wazīf: the shin bone. Al-muʿabbad: the tamed.]]

Al-mawr also means waves. A "nāqa mawwāratu al-yad" is a swift she-camel. A camel's upper arms (ʿaḍudān) "yamūru" when they move back and forth along the side of its body. The poet said:

*On the back of a horse with a rippling flank.*

Al-milāt means the side. And their saying: "I do not know whether he went (ghār) or came back (māra)," meaning whether he went down into the lowland (ghawr) or turned and returned to Najd. Al-mūr, with a dammah, means dust carried by the wind. It was also said: the sky here means the celestial sphere, and its mawr is the disruption of its order and the variation of its movement; this was said by Ibn Bahr.

(And the mountains will move, moving.) Muqatil said: they will move from their places until they become level with the earth. It was also said: they will move as clouds move today in this world. Its explanation is His saying: (And you see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass like the passing of clouds). [[See vol. 13, p. 242.]] This meaning has already been discussed in (al-Kahf). [[See vol. 10, p. 416.]]

(So woe on that Day to the deniers) "Woe" (fa-wayl) is a word said to one who is destined for destruction. The "fa" entered because the sentence carries the meaning of a conditional consequence.

(Who are in an idle plunge, playing) meaning: wandering in falsehood, namely their plunging into the matter of Muhammad with denial. It was also said: plunging into the affairs of the worldly life, playing, not remembering reckoning or recompense. This was already discussed in (al-Bara'a). [[See vol. 8, p. 201.]]

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿On the Day they will be pushed⦆ ("yawm") is a substitute (badal) for "yawmaʾidhin." And (yudaʿʿūna) means they will be pushed into Hell with force and violence. It is said: "daʿaʿtuhu adʿuʿuhu daʿʿan," meaning I pushed him. From this is His saying: ﴿So that is the one who repulses the orphan﴾. [[See vol. 20, p. 211.]] In the exegesis it is said: the guardians of Hell will chain their hands to their necks and gather their forelocks to their feet, then push them into the Fire, pushing them on their faces and thrusting them on their necks until they reach the Fire. Abu Raja al-ʿUtaridi and Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read (on the Day they will be pushed toward the Fire of Hell with a push) with the lightened form, from "al-duʿāʾ" (calling). When they come near the Fire, the guardians will say to them: (This is the Fire which you used to deny) in the worldly life.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is this magic, or do you not see?﴾ This is an interrogative whose meaning is rebuke and reproach. That is, it will be said to them: (Is this magic) which you now see with your own eyes, (or do you not perceive)? It was also said: "am" here means "bal" (rather), meaning: rather, you did not see in the worldly life, nor did you understand.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Burn therein﴾, meaning the guardians will say to them: taste its heat by entering it.

(Whether you endure it or do not endure it, it is the same for you), meaning: whether you have patience in it or not, the outcome is the same. The predicate of "sawāʾ" is omitted, meaning: whether you are distressed or patient, it is equal for you, and nothing will benefit you. This is like what He reported about them, that they say: (It is the same for us whether we are distressed or we are patient). [[See vol. 9, p. 355.]]

(You are only being recompensed for what you used to do).

[[See vol. 20, p. 211.]] In the exegesis it is said: the guardians of Hell will chain their hands to their necks and gather their forelocks to their feet, then push them into the Fire, pushing them on their faces and thrusting them on their necks until they reach the Fire. Abu Raja al-ʿUtaridi and Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read (on the Day they will be pushed toward the Fire of Hell with a push) with the lightened form, from "al-duʿāʾ" (calling). When they come near the Fire, the guardians will say to them: (This is the Fire which you used to deny) in the worldly life.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is this magic, or do you not see?﴾ This is an interrogative whose meaning is rebuke and reproach. That is, it will be said to them: (Is this magic) which you now see with your own eyes, (or do you not perceive)? It was also said: "am" here means "bal" (rather), meaning: rather, you did not see in the worldly life, nor did you understand.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Burn therein﴾, meaning the guardians will say to them: taste its heat by entering it.

(Whether you endure it or do not endure it, it is the same for you), meaning: whether you have patience in it or not, the outcome is the same. The predicate of "sawāʾ" is omitted, meaning: whether you are distressed or patient, it is equal for you, and nothing will benefit you. This is like what He reported about them, that they say: (It is the same for us whether we are distressed or we are patient). [[See vol. 9, p. 355.]]

(You are only being recompensed for what you used to do).

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 52, verses 9–16:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿On the Day when the sky will sway violently﴾. The word that governs "the Day" (yawm) in His saying "will surely occur" means: the punishment will befall them on the Day of Resurrection, and it is the Day on which the sky will sway. The people of lexicography (ahl al-lugha) said: "māra al-shay'u yamūru mawran" means it moved, came and went, as a tall date palm (al-nakhla al-ʿaydāna, i.e., the tall one) sways, and "al-tamawwur" is similar to it. Al-Dahhak said: some of it will surge into others. Mujahid said: it will revolve in a circular motion. Abu Ubayda and al-Akhfash said: it will tilt. He cited al-A'sha:

*As if her gait, from her neighbour's house,*
*Is the drifting of a cloud, neither slow nor hasty.*

It was also said: it will flow in a flowing manner. From this is the saying of Jarir:

*The slain kept their blood flowing in the Tigris,*
*until the water of the Tigris turned reddish-white.* [[al-ashkal: that in which there is whiteness and redness.]]

Ibn ʿAbbas said: on that Day the sky will sway with what is in it and will be agitated. It was also said: its people will revolve in it and some of them will surge into others. Al-mawr also means the road. From this is the saying of Tarafa:

*... over a well-trodden road.* [[The line is from his Mu'allaqa, and its full verse is:*
*They race against swift, noble she-camels, following*
*A sturdy leg over a well-trodden road.*
*Tabari: contending. Al-ʿitaq: noble she-camels. Al-nājiyāt: the swift ones. Al-wazīf: the shin bone. Al-muʿabbad: the tamed.]]

Al-mawr also means waves. A "nāqa mawwāratu al-yad" is a swift she-camel. A camel's upper arms (ʿaḍudān) "yamūru" when they move back and forth along the side of its body. The poet said:

*On the back of a horse with a rippling flank.*

Al-milāt means the side. And their saying: "I do not know whether he went (ghār) or came back (māra)," meaning whether he went down into the lowland (ghawr) or turned and returned to Najd. Al-mūr, with a dammah, means dust carried by the wind. It was also said: the sky here means the celestial sphere, and its mawr is the disruption of its order and the variation of its movement; this was said by Ibn Bahr.

(And the mountains will move, moving.) Muqatil said: they will move from their places until they become level with the earth. It was also said: they will move as clouds move today in this world. Its explanation is His saying: (And you see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass like the passing of clouds). [[See vol. 13, p. 242.]] This meaning has already been discussed in (al-Kahf). [[See vol. 10, p. 416.]]

(So woe on that Day to the deniers) "Woe" (fa-wayl) is a word said to one who is destined for destruction. The "fa" entered because the sentence carries the meaning of a conditional consequence.

(Who are in an idle plunge, playing) meaning: wandering in falsehood, namely their plunging into the matter of Muhammad with denial. It was also said: plunging into the affairs of the worldly life, playing, not remembering reckoning or recompense. This was already discussed in (al-Bara'a). [[See vol. 8, p. 201.]]

(Whether you endure it or do not endure it, it is the same for you), meaning: whether you have patience in it or not, the outcome is the same. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 52, verse 17–20:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and bliss﴾. When He mentioned the condition of the disbelievers, He also mentioned the condition of the believers. (﻿Fakihin) means possessing abundant fruit. It is said: "a man is fakih," meaning possessing fruit, just as it is said: laban and tamar, meaning possessing milk and dates. [The poet said, the poet being al-Hutay'ah]:

"You deceived me and claimed that you / are laban in summer, tamir"

meaning possessing milk and dates. Al-Hasan and others read (fakihin) without an alif, and its meaning, according to Ibn 'Abbas and others, is joyful and luxuriating. It is said: "fakiha al-rajul" with a kasra, so he is fakih, if he is good-natured and jocular. Al-fakih also means arrogant and insolent. The discussion of this has already passed in (al-Dukhan) [see vol. 16, p. 139].

(Bima atahum) meaning: what their Lord gave them, ﴿and their Lord protected them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire﴾.

(Kulu washrabu) meaning: it will be said to them.

(Hani'an) The hani' is that which has no troubling, no spoiling, and no turbidity. Al-Zajjaj said: meaning, may what you have arrived at be pleasant for you (hani'an). It was also said: meaning, you were given the enjoyment of the bliss of Paradise, a pleasant enjoyment. It was also said: meaning, eat and drink, you have been made happy (hani'tum), so (hani'an) is an adjective in the place of the verbal noun. It was also said: (hani'an) means lawful. It was said: no harm in it and no hidden danger. It was also said: (hani'an) means you will not die, for whatever does not last, or after which a person does not remain, is a troubled thing, not a pleasant one.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Reclining on couches arranged in rows﴾. Sururun is the plural of sarir. In the speech there is an ellipsis; its estimate is: reclining on cushions upon couches.

(Masfufatin). Ibn al-A'rabi said: meaning joined one to another until they become a row. Reports say that they are arranged in the sky at such and such a length; when the servant wishes to sit upon them, they lower themselves for him, and when he sits upon them, they return to their state. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are couches of gold, adorned with chrysolite, pearls, and rubies, and the sarir is the distance between Makkah and Aylah.

(Wa zawwajnahum bihur 'in) meaning: We paired them with them. Yunus ibn Habib said: the Arabs say "zawwajtuhu imra'atan" and "tazawwajtu imra'atan," and it is not from the speech of the Arabs to say "tazawwajtu bi-imra'atin." He said: the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, (wa zawwajnahum bihur 'in), meaning: We paired them with them, is from the saying of Allah, exalted is He: (Gather those who did wrong and their spouses), meaning and their companions. Al-Farra' said: "tazawwajtu bi-imra'atin" is a dialect of the Azd Shanu'ah. The discussion of the meaning of al-hur al-'in has already passed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 52, verse 21–24:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith﴾. The common readers (al-'Amma) read (wa-ittaba'athum) with a connecting alif, a doubled ta', an open 'ayn and a sukun on the ta'. 'Amr read (wa-atba'nahum) with a cutting alif, a sukun on the ta' and the 'ayn, and a nun, in consideration of His saying (alhaqna bihim), so that the discourse follows one pattern. As for His saying (dhurriyyatuhum) the first time, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it in the plural, and it was transmitted from Nafi' likewise, except that Abu 'Amr vowelled the ta' with a kasra as a passive, while the rest vowelled it with a damma. The rest read (dhurriyyatuhum) in the singular with a damma on the ta', and this is the well-known reading from Nafi'. As for the second, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with a kasra on the ta' in the plural. The rest read (dhurriyyatahum) in the singular with a fatha on the ta'.

Its meaning has been disputed. Four narrations are reported from Ibn 'Abbas. The first: he said, "Allah certainly raises the offspring of the believer to be with him in his rank in Paradise, even if they fall short of him in deeds, so that his eye may be delighted by them," and he recited this verse. al-Nahhas related it in marfu' form in his book (al-Nasikh wa'l-Mansukh) from Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, raises the offspring of the believer to be with him in his rank in Paradise, even if he did not reach it by his deeds, so that his eye may be delighted by them." Then he recited, "And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith…" the verse. Abu Ja'far said: Thus the hadith becomes marfu' to the Prophet ﷺ, and so it must be, for Ibn 'Abbas would not say this except from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, since it is an informing about what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does, and in the sense that He revealed it, may His praise be exalted. al-Zamakhshari said: So Allah gathers for them all kinds of joy: their happiness within themselves, the marriage to the wide-eyed houris (al-Hur al-'In), the companionship of their believing brethren, and the gathering of their children and descendants with them.

Also from Ibn 'Abbas: he said, "Allah certainly joins to the believer his offspring, the young children who have not reached faith," as stated by al-Mahdawi. The term dhurriyyah applies to both the young and the adult. If dhurriyyah here is taken to mean the young, then His saying (bi-imanin) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the two objects, and the implied meaning is "with faith from the fathers." If dhurriyyah is taken to mean the adults, then His saying (bi-imanin) is a circumstantial clause relating to the agents.

The third saying from Ibn 'Abbas: the intended meaning of "those who believed" is the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun) and the Helpers (al-Ansar), and "the offspring" are the Successors (al-Tabi'un). In another narration from him: if the fathers are higher in rank, Allah raises the sons to the fathers; and if the sons are higher in rank, Allah raises the fathers to the sons. Thus the fathers are included within the word dhurriyyah, as in His saying: (And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship). Also from Ibn 'Abbas, raising it to the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, one of them asks about his parents, his wife and his child, and it is said to them: 'They did not attain what you attained.' He says: 'O Lord, I worked for myself and for them.' So it is commanded that they be joined to him."

(Khadijah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: I asked the Prophet ﷺ about two sons of mine who died in the Jahiliyyah, and he said to me: "They are in the Fire." When he saw the aversion in my face, he said: "If you saw their place, you would hate them." She said: "O Messenger of Allah, and my child by you?" He said: "In Paradise." Then he said: "Indeed the believers and their children are in Paradise, and the polytheists and their children are in the Fire." [[This hadith came before his saying ﷺ: "I asked my Lord and He gave me the children of the polytheists as servants for the people of Paradise."]]) Then he recited, "And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith…" the verse.

(And We did not deprive them of anything of their deeds) meaning: We did not diminish the children from the reward of their deeds because of the shortness of their lives, nor did We diminish the fathers from the reward of their deeds by joining their offspring to them. The pronoun (hum) refers back to His saying "And those who believed." Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is "and their offspring followed them in faith" — We joined to the offspring their young sons who had not reached the age of deeds; so according to this view the pronoun refers to the offspring. Ibn Kathir read (wa-ma alatnahum) with a kasra on the lam; the rest read it with a fatha. From Abu Hurayrah: (alatnahum) with a madd. Ibn al-A'rabi said: alatahu yalituhu altan, and a'latahu yu'liituhu ila'tan, and latahu yaliituhu laytan — all of these mean "he diminished him."

In al-Sihah: latahu 'an wajhihi yalutuhu and yaliituhu, meaning he held him back from his direction and turned him aside; likewise a'lathu 'an wajhihi, fa'ala and af'ala being of one meaning. It is also said: ma alatahu min 'amalihi shay'an, meaning he did not diminish him, like "altahu" — and this has passed in (al-Hujurat) [[See vol. 16, p. 348]].

(Every person is held in pledge for what he has earned.) It was said: this refers to the people of Hell. Ibn 'Abbas said: the people of Hell are held in pledge by their deeds, while the people of Paradise go to their bliss; and for this He says: "Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned, except the companions of the right" [[See vol. 19, p. 85]]. It was also said: it is general for every human being, held in pledge by his deed, so no one is diminished from the reward of his deed; but any increase beyond the reward of the deed is a bounty from Allah. It is possible that this applies to the offspring who did not believe, so they do not join their believing fathers, but remain held in pledge by their disbelief.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We provided them with fruit and meat of whatever they desire﴾, meaning: We increased for them of that, an additional gift from Allah, providing them with what was not theirs before.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They pass to one another therein a cup﴾, meaning: some of them take it from others, namely the believer, his wives and his servants in Paradise. The kas is the vessel of wine, and every vessel filled with drink or other things; when it is emptied it is no longer called a kas. The evidence for "tanazu'" and "al-kas" in the language is the saying of al-Akhtal:

"A drinker who slaughters the young camels for his guests, who has filled the cup and reproached me, / Not stingy nor narrow-hearted nor a brawler…" [[Commentary note from the edition: the verse as cited is "wa-shari'in mufrihin bi'l-ka's nadamani..."]]

"I contended with him for the pure, mature wine, when the rooster crowed and the hour of the night traveller arrived."

And Imru' al-Qays said:

"When we contended in talk and it turned pleasant, I bent down a branch with clustered fruit, drooping."

This has been discussed under (al-Saffat) [[See vol. 15, p. 77, where the discussion of the cup is found.]].

(No idle talk therein) meaning: in the cup, that is, no idle talk passes among them. (Nor sinful speech) meaning: nothing in which there is sin. Ta'thim is a form from ithm, meaning that cup does not make them sinners, since it is permitted to them. It was also said: (no idle talk therein) meaning: in Paradise. Ibn 'Ata' said: What idle talk could there be in an assembly whose place is the Garden of Eden, whose cupbearers are the angels, whose drinking is in the remembrance of Allah, whose fragrance and greeting come from Allah, and whose people are the guests of Allah! (And We did not deprive them of anything of their deeds) meaning: We did not diminish the children from the reward of their deeds because of the shortness of their lives, nor did We diminish the fathers from the reward of their deeds by joining their offspring to them. The pronoun (hum) refers back to His saying "And those who believed." Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is "and their offspring followed them in faith" — We joined to the offspring their young sons who had not reached the age of deeds; so according to this view the pronoun refers to the offspring. Ibn Kathir read (wa-ma alatnahum) with a kasra on the lam; the rest read it with a fatha. From Abu Hurayrah: (alatnahum) with a madd. Ibn al-A'rabi said: alatahu yalituhu altan, and a'latahu yu'liituhu ila'tan, and latahu yaliituhu laytan — all of these mean "he diminished him."

In al-Sihah: latahu 'an wajhihi yalutuhu and yaliituhu, meaning he held him back from his direction and turned him aside; likewise a'lathu 'an wajhihi, fa'ala and af'ala being of one meaning. It is also said: ma alatahu min 'amalihi shay'an, meaning he did not diminish him, like "altahu" — and this has passed in (al-Hujurat) [[See vol. 16, p. 348]].

(Every person is held in pledge for what he has earned.) It was said: this refers to the people of Hell. Ibn 'Abbas said: the people of Hell are held in pledge by their deeds, while the people of Paradise go to their bliss; and for this He says: "Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned, except the companions of the right" [[See vol. 19, p. 85]]. It was also said: it is general for every human being, held in pledge by his deed, so no one is diminished from the reward of his deed; but any increase beyond the reward of the deed is a bounty from Allah. It is possible that this applies to the offspring who did not believe, so they do not join their believing fathers, but remain held in pledge by their disbelief.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We provided them with fruit and meat of whatever they desire﴾, meaning: We increased for them of that, an additional gift from Allah, providing them with what was not theirs before.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They pass to one another therein a cup﴾, meaning: some of them take it from others, namely the believer, his wives and his servants in Paradise. The kas is the vessel of wine, and every vessel filled with drink or other things; when it is emptied it is no longer called a kas. The evidence for "tanazu'" and "al-kas" in the language is the saying of al-Akhtal:

"A drinker who slaughters the young camels for his guests, who has filled the cup and reproached me, / Not stingy nor narrow-hearted nor a brawler…" [[Commentary note from the edition: the verse as cited is "wa-shari'in mufrihin bi'l-ka's nadamani..."]]

"I contended with him for the pure, mature wine, when the rooster crowed and the hour of the night traveller arrived."

And Imru' al-Qays said:

"When we contended in talk and it turned pleasant, I bent down a branch with clustered fruit, drooping."

This has been discussed under (al-Saffat) [[See vol. 15, p. 77, where the discussion of the cup is found.]].

(No idle talk therein) meaning: in the cup, that is, no idle talk passes among them. (Nor sinful speech) meaning: nothing in which there is sin. Ta'thim is a form from ithm, meaning that cup does not make them sinners, since it is permitted to them. It was also said: (no idle talk therein) meaning: in Paradise. Ibn 'Ata' said: What idle talk could there be in an assembly whose place is the Garden of Eden, whose cupbearers are the angels, whose drinking is in the remembrance of Allah, whose fragrance and greeting come from Allah, and whose people are the guests of Allah! (Nor sinful speech) meaning: nor lying, as said by Ibn 'Abbas. al-Dahhak: meaning none of them calls another a liar. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin and Abu 'Amr read (la laghwun fiha wa-la ta'thimun) with a fatha on the final letter; the rest read it with a damma and tanwin. This has passed in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 3, p. 267]] at His saying: (Nor friendship, nor intercession), and all praise is due to Allah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And there will circulate among them young servants of theirs﴾, meaning: with fruits, delicacies, food and drink. Its evidence is: (They are circulated among with dishes of gold) [[See vol. 16, p. 111]], (They are circulated among with a cup from a flowing spring) [[See vol. 15, p. 77]]. Then it was said: they are the young children of theirs who died before them, whom Allah thus delights their eyes with. It was also said: they are those whom Allah has made to serve them from the children of others. It was also said: they are servants created in Paradise. al-Kalbi said: they never grow old, (as if they were) in beauty and whiteness (pearls well-guarded), in the shell, and al-maknun means the protected. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿There circulate among them everlasting youths﴾ [[See p. 202 of this volume.]]. It was said: they are the children of the polytheists, and they are servants of the people of Paradise. There is no toil in Paradise and no need for service, but He informs that they are at the height of bliss. From 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her: the Prophet of Allah ﷺ said: "The lowest in rank among the people of Paradise is one who calls his servant from among his servants, and a thousand answer him, all saying: 'Here I am, here I am!'" From 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, who said: the Prophet ﷺ said: "There is none among the people of Paradise but that a thousand young servants run before him, each one engaged in a task that his companion is not engaged in." From al-Hasan, that they said: "O Messenger of Allah, if the servant is like a pearl, how then is the one served?" He said: "The difference between them is like the difference between the moon on the night of its fullness and the smallest of the stars." al-Kisa'i said: kanantu al-shay' means I concealed it and protected it from the sun; and akananthu fi nafsi means I kept it secret. Abu Zayd said: kannatuhu and akannatuhu have the same meaning, both in covering and in the mind; you say: kannat al-'ilm and akannatuhu, so it is maknun and mukann. And kannat al-jariyah and akannatuha, so she is maknunah and mukannah.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 52, verse 25–28:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will turn to one another, questioning each other﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: when they are raised from their graves, some of them will ask others. It was also said: in Paradise, (yatasa'alun) means they will recall what they had endured in the world of toil and fear of the outcome, and they will praise God, exalted is He, for the removal of fear from them. It was also said: one of them will say to another, "By what did you reach this lofty station?" ﴿They will say, "Indeed, we were before this among our people, fearful [of God]."﴾ That is, each one questioned among them said to his questioner: "Indeed, we were before" (qabl), meaning in the world, "fearful and apprehensive of the punishment of God."

﴿So God has bestowed favor upon us﴾ with Paradise and forgiveness. It was also said: with success (tawfiq) and guidance.

﴿And has protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind (as-samum)﴾. Al-Hasan said: "as-Samum" is one of the names of the Fire and one of the levels of Hell. It was also said: it is the Fire itself, just as one says "Jahannam." It was also said: it is the punishment-fire of as-Samum. As-Samum is the hot wind, and it is feminine. It is said of it: "Our day was samum, so it is masmum," and its plural is sama'im. Abu Ubayda said: as-Samum occurs by day and may occur by night, while al-Haruru occurs by night and may occur by day; and as-Samum may be used for the scorching of cold [and that is in the increase from the manuscript n.] the scorching of heat, and the sun is more so. The reciter (ar-rajiz) said:

"Today is a day whose samum is cold; whoever despairs today, I will not blame him."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, we used to call upon Him before﴾, that is, in the world, asking Him to bestow forgiveness upon us for our shortcomings. It was also said: (nadʿuhu) means we used to worship Him.

﴿Indeed, He is the Good, the Merciful﴾. Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read (annahu) with a fathah on the hamzah, meaning "because He is." The rest read it with a kasrah, as a new sentence. Al-Barr means al-Latif (the Subtle, Gracious), as Ibn ʿAbbas said. It is also related from him that it means the one who is true to what He promised. Ibn Jurayj said likewise.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 52, verse 29–34:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So remind, for by the grace of your Lord you are not a soothsayer, nor a madman﴾. That is, so remind, O Muhammad, your people with the Quran.

(By the grace of your Lord) meaning by the message of your Lord, (you are not a soothsayer) who invents speech and reports what will happen tomorrow without revelation, (nor a madman).

This is a refutation of their saying about the Prophet ﷺ. ʿUqba ibn Abi Muʿayt said he was a madman, Shayba ibn Rabiʿa said he was a sorcerer, and others said he was a soothsayer. So Allah, exalted is He, declared them liars and refuted them. Then it was said: the meaning of (by the grace of your Lord) is an oath, that is, and by the grace of Allah you are neither a soothsayer nor a madman. And it was said: it is not an oath, but rather it is like your saying: "You are not, by the praise of Allah, ignorant," meaning that Allah has cleared you of that.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do they say, "A poet"?﴾ That is, rather they say, "Muhammad is a poet." Sibawayh said: the servants were addressed in terms of what was current in their speech. Abu Jaʿfar al-Nahhas said: this is a good statement, but it is not explained or elaborated. Sibawayh means that (am) in the speech of the Arabs is used for transition from one discourse to another, as the poet [[It is al-Aʿsha.]] said:

Do you forsake a beautiful woman, or does she not concern you?

Then the speech was complete, and then he moved on to something else, saying:

Or is the rope, with her, broken and severed?

What comes in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, of this kind has the meaning of affirmation, reproach, and transition from one discourse to another, and the grammarians illustrate it with (bal, rather).

(We await for him the vicissitudes of fate.) Qatada said: some of the disbelievers said, "Wait for Muhammad's death; it will suffice you as it sufficed the poet of such-and-such a clan." Al-Dahhak said: these are the Banu ʿAbd al-Dar, who attributed to him that he is a poet, meaning he will perish soon as those poets before him perished, and that his father died young, so he may die as his father died. Al-Akhfash said: "we await for him" means "until the vicissitudes of fate," and the preposition was omitted, as you say: "I aimed at Zayd" and "I aimed toward Zayd." Al-Manun, according to Ibn ʿAbbas, is death. Abu al-Ghawl al-Tuhawi said:

They defended the sanctuary of al-Waqba with a blow that joins together the scattered fates (al-manun).

[[He is from the Banu Nahshal, and his name is ʿAlbaʾ ibn Jawshan. Al-Waqba is, like Jumzā, a water of the Banu Malik ibn Mazin, famous for many battles, and it is on the road from Basra to Madina.]]

That is, the deaths. He says: the blow joins together people scattered in places; if their deaths came to them in their places, they would be scattered, so they gathered in one place and their deaths came to them gathered together. Al-Suddi said, from Abu Malik, from Ibn ʿAbbas: (rayb) in the Quran means doubt, except in one place in al-Tur, (rayb al-manun) means the calamities of affairs. The poet [[In the manuscripts of the original: "Ibn ʿAbbas said," and this is not right; in the rest of the books of tafsir it says "the poet said," as we have recorded it.]] said:

Wait for her the vicissitudes of fate, perhaps she will be divorced one day or her husband will die.

Mujahid said: (rayb al-manun) means the calamities of time, and al-manun is time. Abu Dhuʾayb said:

Do you grieve because of fate and its vicissitudes, while time does not reproach the one who laments?

Al-Aʿsha said:

Did he see a crooked man whom the vicissitudes of fate and a wasting, afflicting time struck? [[It is narrated: "and a time that is ruined" (mufannid). That is the well-known transmission. Mutbil means wasting or taking away family and children. Khabal, like kataf, means twisted against his family, with no good seen in him.]]

Al-Asmaʿi said: al-manun is also the night and the day, and they were named so because they diminish lifespans and cut off terms. It is also reported from him that time was called manun because it takes away the vigor of living beings, that is their strength, and likewise al-maniyya. Abu ʿUbayda said: time was called manun because it weakens, from their saying "a thin rope" (habl manin), that is weak, and al-manin is weak dust. Al-Farra said: al-manun is feminine and can be singular or plural. Al-Asmaʿi said: al-manun is singular with no plural. Al-Akhfash said: it is plural with no singular, and al-manun can be masculine or feminine; whoever makes it masculine takes it as time or death, and whoever makes it feminine does so by treating it according to the meaning, as if he intended al-maniyya.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Wait; indeed I am with you among those who wait."﴾ That is, say to them, O Muhammad: wait, that is, expect.

(Indeed I am with you among those who wait) meaning among those who await punishment for you. They were punished on the day of Badr by the sword.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do their minds command them to this?﴾ That is, their intellects (to this), that is, to lie against you.

(Or are they a transgressing people?) That is, or did they transgress without intellects? It was also said: (am) means (bal), that is, rather they disbelieved out of rebellion even though the truth became manifest to them. It was said to ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs: what is the matter with your people that they did not believe, when Allah described them as having intellect? He said: those are intellects that Allah has deceived, that is, He did not accompany them with success. It was also said: (ahlamuhum) means their minds, because intellect is not given to the disbeliever; if he had intellect he would have believed. Rather the disbeliever is given the mind, and so it became a proof against him. The mind accepts knowledge in general, while intellect discerns knowledge and measures the proportions of the limits of command and prohibition. It is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, how intelligent is that Christian so-and-so!" He said: "Enough. The disbeliever has no intellect. Have you not heard the saying of Allah, exalted is He: 'And they said, if we had listened or reasoned, we would not have been among the companions of the Blaze'?" And in the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar: the Prophet ﷺ rebuked him, then said: "Enough, for the intelligent one is the one who acts in obedience to Allah." Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim Abu ʿAbd Allah mentioned it with its chain.

(Or do they say, "He has fabricated it"?) That is, he invented and forged it, meaning the Quran. Taqawwul is the affectation of speech, and it is used mostly for lying. It is said: "qawwaltani ma lam aqul" and "aqwaltani ma lam aqul," meaning you claimed it against me. "Taqawwala ʿalayhi" means he lied against him. "Iqtala ʿalayhi" means he ruled arbitrarily over him. The poet [[He is Kaʿb ibn Saʿd al-Ghanawi.]] said:

A station in a house of truth and ease, and what was decreed against me by an arbitrary ruler is no physician.

So the first (am) is for denial, and the second is for affirmation, meaning: it is not as they say.

(Rather they do not believe) out of denial and arrogance.

(Then let them produce a discourse like it) that is, a Quran resembling it, from their own selves (if they are truthful) that Muhammad forged it. Al-Jahdari read (fa-li-yaʾtū bi-ḥadīthin mithlihi) with the genitive construction. The pronoun in (mithlihi) refers to the Prophet ﷺ, and the discourse that is meant as the Quran is attributed to him because he is the one sent with it. On the reading of the majority, the pronoun refers to the Quran.

This is a refutation of their saying about the Prophet ﷺ. ʿUqba ibn Abi Muʿayt said he was a madman, Shayba ibn Rabiʿa said he was a sorcerer, and others said he was a soothsayer. So Allah, exalted is He, declared them liars and refuted them. Then it was said: the meaning of (by the grace of your Lord) is an oath, that is, and by the grace of Allah you are neither a soothsayer nor a madman. And it was said: it is not an oath, but rather it is like your saying: "You are not, by the praise of Allah, ignorant," meaning that Allah has cleared you of that.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do they say, "A poet"?﴾ That is, rather they say, "Muhammad is a poet." Sibawayh said: the servants were addressed in terms of what was current in their speech. Abu Jaʿfar al-Nahhas said: this is a good statement, but it is not explained or elaborated. Sibawayh means that (am) in the speech of the Arabs is used for transition from one discourse to another, as the poet [[It is al-Aʿsha.]] said:

Do you forsake a beautiful woman, or does she not concern you?

Then the speech was complete, and then he moved on to something else, saying:

Or is the rope, with her, broken and severed?

What comes in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, of this kind has the meaning of affirmation, reproach, and transition from one discourse to another, and the grammarians illustrate it with (bal, rather).

(We await for him the vicissitudes of fate.) Qatada said: some of the disbelievers said, "Wait for Muhammad's death; it will suffice you as it sufficed the poet of such-and-such a clan." Al-Dahhak said: these are the Banu ʿAbd al-Dar, who attributed to him that he is a poet, meaning he will perish soon as those poets before him perished, and that his father died young, so he may die as his father died. Al-Akhfash said: "we await for him" means "until the vicissitudes of fate," and the preposition was omitted, as you say: "I aimed at Zayd" and "I aimed toward Zayd." Al-Manun, according to Ibn ʿAbbas, is death. Abu al-Ghawl al-Tuhawi said:

They defended the sanctuary of al-Waqba with a blow that joins together the scattered fates (al-manun).

[[He is from the Banu Nahshal, and his name is ʿAlbaʾ ibn Jawshan. Al-Waqba is, like Jumzā, a water of the Banu Malik ibn Mazin, famous for many battles, and it is on the road from Basra to Madina.]]

That is, the deaths. He says: the blow joins together people scattered in places; if their deaths came to them in their places, they would be scattered, so they gathered in one place and their deaths came to them gathered together. Al-Suddi said, from Abu Malik, from Ibn ʿAbbas: (rayb) in the Quran means doubt, except in one place in al-Tur, (rayb al-manun) means the calamities of affairs. The poet [[In the manuscripts of the original: "Ibn ʿAbbas said," and this is not right; in the rest of the books of tafsir it says "the poet said," as we have recorded it.]] said:

Wait for her the vicissitudes of fate, perhaps she will be divorced one day or her husband will die.

Mujahid said: (rayb al-manun) means the calamities of time, and al-manun is time. Abu Dhuʾayb said:

Do you grieve because of fate and its vicissitudes, while time does not reproach the one who laments?

Al-Aʿsha said:

Did he see a crooked man whom the vicissitudes of fate and a wasting, afflicting time struck? [[It is narrated: "and a time that is ruined" (mufannid). That is the well-known transmission. Mutbil means wasting or taking away family and children. Khabal, like kataf, means twisted against his family, with no good seen in him.]]

Al-Asmaʿi said: al-manun is also the night and the day, and they were named so because they diminish lifespans and cut off terms. It is also reported from him that time was called manun because it takes away the vigor of living beings, that is their strength, and likewise al-maniyya. Abu ʿUbayda said: time was called manun because it weakens, from their saying "a thin rope" (habl manin), that is weak, and al-manin is weak dust. Al-Farra said: al-manun is feminine and can be singular or plural. Al-Asmaʿi said: al-manun is singular with no plural. Al-Akhfash said: it is plural with no singular, and al-manun can be masculine or feminine; whoever makes it masculine takes it as time or death, and whoever makes it feminine does so by treating it according to the meaning, as if he intended al-maniyya.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Wait; indeed I am with you among those who wait."﴾ That is, say to them, O Muhammad: wait, that is, expect.

(Indeed I am with you among those who wait) meaning among those who await punishment for you. They were punished on the day of Badr by the sword.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do their minds command them to this?﴾ That is, their intellects (to this), that is, to lie against you.

(Or are they a transgressing people?) That is, or did they transgress without intellects? It was also said: (am) means (bal), that is, rather they disbelieved out of rebellion even though the truth became manifest to them. It was said to ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs: what is the matter with your people that they did not believe, when Allah described them as having intellect? He said: those are intellects that Allah has deceived, that is, He did not accompany them with success. It was also said: (ahlamuhum) means their minds, because intellect is not given to the disbeliever; if he had intellect he would have believed. Rather the disbeliever is given the mind, and so it became a proof against him. The mind accepts knowledge in general, while intellect discerns knowledge and measures the proportions of the limits of command and prohibition. It is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, how intelligent is that Christian so-and-so!" He said: "Enough. The disbeliever has no intellect. Have you not heard the saying of Allah, exalted is He: 'And they said, if we had listened or reasoned, we would not have been among the companions of the Blaze'?" And in the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar: the Prophet ﷺ rebuked him, then said: "Enough, for the intelligent one is the one who acts in obedience to Allah." Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim Abu ʿAbd Allah mentioned it with its chain.

(Or do they say, "He has fabricated it"?) That is, he invented and forged it, meaning the Quran. Taqawwul is the affectation of speech, and it is used mostly for lying. It is said: "qawwaltani ma lam aqul" and "aqwaltani ma lam aqul," meaning you claimed it against me. "Taqawwala ʿalayhi" means he lied against him. "Iqtala ʿalayhi" means he ruled arbitrarily over him. The poet [[He is Kaʿb ibn Saʿd al-Ghanawi.]] said:

A station in a house of truth and ease, and what was decreed against me by an arbitrary ruler is no physician.

So the first (am) is for denial, and the second is for affirmation, meaning: it is not as they say.

(Rather they do not believe) out of denial and arrogance.

(Then let them produce a discourse like it) that is, a Quran resembling it, from their own selves (if they are truthful) that Muhammad forged it. Al-Jahdari read (fa-li-yaʾtū bi-ḥadīthin mithlihi) with the genitive construction. The pronoun in (mithlihi) refers to the Prophet ﷺ, and the discourse that is meant as the Quran is attributed to him because he is the one sent with it. On the reading of the majority, the pronoun refers to the Quran.

The Exalted said: ﴿Or were they created from nothing?﴾ (*Am*) is an extra particle (*sila za'ida*), and the sense is: "Were they created from nothing?" (*akhuliqu min ghayr shay'*). Ibn 'Abbas said: "From nothing, with no Lord who created and ordained them." It was also said: "From neither mother nor father, so they are like inanimate matter, who do not reason, and against whom no proof from God would stand." [They are] not like that. Were they not created from a drop of semen, a clinging clot, and a lump of flesh? This was said by Ibn 'Ata'. Ibn Kaysan said: "Were they created in vain and left neglected (*sudan*)?" (*min ghayr shay'*), meaning "for no purpose," so *min* carries the sense of *li* (for).

﴿Or are they the creators?﴾ That is, do they claim that they created themselves, so that they would not obey God's command? They do not say this. And since they acknowledge that there is a Creator other than themselves, what prevents them from affirming Him alone in worship, rather than the idols, and from affirming that He is capable of resurrection?

﴿Or did they create the heavens and the earth?﴾ That is, the matter is not so; they have created nothing. ﴿Rather, they are not certain﴾ of the truth.

﴿Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord?﴾ That is, do they possess that, so that they would be independent of God and turn away from His command? Ibn 'Abbas said: "The treasuries of your Lord are rain and provision." It was also said: "They are the keys of mercy." 'Ikrimah said: "They are prophethood," meaning: "Do the keys of your Lord, with respect to the message, lie in their hands, so that they may place them wherever they wish?" The comparison with treasuries is drawn because a *khizana* (treasury) is a room prepared to gather various kinds of stored goods, and the capacities of the Lord are like the treasuries that contain every kind, so they have no end.

﴿Or are they the controllers?﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: "Those who hold power, the tyrants." From him also: "The falsifiers." This was also said by al-Dahhak. From Ibn 'Abbas also: "Or are they the guardians?" 'Ata': "Or are they lords who dominate?" 'Ata' said: It is said *tasaytarta 'alayya*, meaning "you made me your servant." Abu 'Ubayda also said this. In *al-Sihah* [of al-Jawhari]: *al-musaytir* and *al-musaytir* are one who is empowered over a thing in order to oversee it, look after its affairs, and record its deeds; its root is from *al-sattr* (line), because the book is written in lines (*yusattaru*), and the one who does this is *musattir* and *musaytir*. It is said: *saytarta 'alayna*. Ibn Bahr said: "Or are they the *al-musaytirun*," that is, they are the guardians, derived from writing lines in a book that preserves what is written in it, so that *al-musaytir* here means one who preserves what God has written in the Preserved Tablet. There are three dialectal forms: with *sad* (which the common readers recite), with *sin* (the reading of Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, Mujahid, Qunbul, Hisham and Abu Hayawa), and with *sad* inclining toward *zay* (the reading of Hamza, as already mentioned under *al-sirat*).[[See vol. 1 p. ...]]

The Exalted said: ﴿Or do they have a ladder﴾, that is, do they claim that they have a means of ascent to the heaven, a route and a way, ﴿by which they listen﴾, that is, by which they hear the news and reach knowledge of the unseen, just as Muhammad ﷺ reaches it through the way of revelation?

﴿Then let their listener bring a clear authority﴾, that is, a manifest proof that what they are upon is true. The *sullam* is the singular of *salalim*, the steps by which one ascends. It may also be called *ghars* (a peg). Abu al-Ra'is al-Tha'labi, describing his she-camel, said:

*A quick-moving one, if its rider bends the leg / at a kneeling place, with a ladder of pegs that hastens to it.*

Zuhayr said:

*Whoever fears the causes of death will meet it, / even if he seeks the causes of heaven with a ladder.*

[Variant reading: "Whoever fears the causes of death will be reached by them" (*yanlunahu*), which is the well-known transmission.]

Another said:

*You accused me of a sin, though I did not commit it, / so that you might take an excuse to desert me as a ladder.*

Ibn Muqbil said in the plural:

*The regions of the lands do not protect a man, / nor are ladders built for him in the heavens.*

*Al-ahja'* means the regions, like *al-arja'*; its singular is *hajan* and *raja*, and it is a shortened form. It is also transmitted as *a'nan al-bilad*; *al-a'nan* also means sides and regions, its singular being *'inw* with a kasra. Ibn al-A'rabi said: its singular is *'anan* (shortened). It is said *ja'ana a'na'un min al-nas*, whose singular is *'inw*, and they are groups from various tribes.

﴿By which they listen﴾, that is, *'alayh* (upon it), like the Exalted's words: ﴿upon the trunks of palm trees﴾ [[See vol. 11 p. 224]], that is, upon them. This was said by al-Akhfash. Abu 'Ubayda said: "They listen with it." Al-Zajjaj said: "That is, do they have something like Gabriel, who brings revelation to the Prophet ﷺ?"

The Exalted said: ﴿Or has He daughters while you have sons?﴾ This rebukes their intellects, as a reproach and a rebuke: "Do you attribute daughters to God, while you yourselves are repelled by them?" Whoever has such intellect should not be thought unlikely to deny resurrection.

﴿Or do you ask them for a wage?﴾, that is, for conveying the message.

﴿So they are burdened by debt﴾, that is, they are burdened by the debt you demand of them, [so that] they are strained by what you have obligated them to.

﴿Or do they have the unseen, so that they write it down?﴾ That is, they write down for people whatever they wish of the knowledge of the hidden things. It was also said: that is, do they have knowledge of what is hidden from people, so that they know that what the Messenger told them about the Last Day, Paradise, Hell and resurrection is false? Qatada said: When they said, "We await for him the vicissitudes of time" [Qur'an 52:30], God the Exalted said: ﴿Or do they have the unseen﴾, so that they know when Muhammad will die, or where his affair will end. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Or do they have the Preserved Tablet, so that they write down what is in it and inform people of what is in it?" Al-Qutabi said: "*Yaktubun* means *yahkumun* (judge), and *al-kitab* means judgment; from this is the Exalted's words: ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ [[See vol. 6 p. 435]], that is, He has judged; and His words, peace be upon him: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, I will certainly judge between you by the Book of God,' that is, by the judgment of God."

The Exalted said: ﴿Or do they intend a plot?﴾, that is, a scheme against you in the Abode of Assembly (*dar al-nadwa*).

﴿Then those who disbelieve, they are the ones who will be plotted against﴾, that is, those against whom the scheme is made. ﴿And the evil scheme does not encompass anyone but its own people﴾ [[See vol. 14 p. 358]]. This happened because they were killed at Badr.

﴿Or do they have a god other than God?﴾ One who creates, provides and prevents.

﴿Glory be to God above what they associate with Him﴾: He declared Himself free of having any partner. Al-Khalil said: "Everything in the Surah of *al-Tur* that mentions *am* is an interrogative word, and not a conjunction."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 52, verses 44–46:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if they should see a fragment of the sky falling﴾. He said this in reply to their saying: (So make a fragment of the sky fall upon us) [[See vol. 13, p. (136)]], and their saying: (Or you cause the sky to fall upon us in fragments, as you claimed) [[See vol. 10, p. (33)]]. So He informed that if He did that, they would say: (It is a heaped-up cloud), meaning, some of it piled upon some, which fell upon us, and it is not sky. This is the act of the obstinate one, or the act of one whom imitation (taqlid) has overcome, and both kinds existed among the polytheists. Al-kisaf is the plural of kisfah, which is a piece of something. It is said: "Give me a kisfah of your garment." It is also said in its plural: kisf. It is said: al-kisf and al-kisfah are one and the same. Al-Akhfash said: whoever reads (kisfan) makes it singular, and whoever reads (kisafan) makes it plural. The discussion of this has already preceded in (Subhan) [[See vol. 10, p. (33)]] and elsewhere, and praise be to God.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So leave them﴾ is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

(Until they meet their day in which they will be struck senseless) — with a fatha on the yā', the reading of the majority. Ibn ʿĀmir and ʿĀṣim read it with a ḍammah. Al-Farrāʾ said: they are two dialects, ṣaʿiqa and ṣuʿiqa, like saʿida and suʿida. Qatadah said: the day they die. It was said: it is the Day of Badr. It was said: the Day of the first Blast [[In n: (Another said: at the first Blast).]]. It was said: the Day of Resurrection, in which there will come to them from the punishment what removes their intellects. It was also said: (yuṣʿaqūn) with a ḍammah on the yā', from aṣʿaqahu Allah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The day their plot will avail them nothing at all﴾, meaning, what they plotted against the Prophet (ﷺ) in the world.

(Nor will they be helped) by God. And (yawma) is in the accusative as a substitute for (yawmahumu alladhi fihi yuṣʿaqūn).

**His words, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, for those who have done wrong﴾**, i.e., those who disbelieved, **(a punishment short of that)**. It was said: before their death. Ibn Zayd said: the calamities of this world, such as pains, sicknesses, afflictions, and the loss of wealth and children. Mujahid said: it is hunger and hardship for seven years. Ibn Abbas said: it is killing. He also reported from him: the punishment of the grave. Al-Bara' ibn Azib and Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, said the same. So **(dun)** here means **ghayr** (other than). It was also said: a punishment lighter than the punishment of the Hereafter.

Some scholars interpreted the verse according to this view as recommended (*nadb*), and considered it abrogated by the five daily prayers. It was reported from al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd that His words **(and at the retreat of the stars)** intend the dawn prayer, and this is the choice of al-Tabari. It was reported from Ibn Abbas that it is the glorification at the end of the prayers.

With a kasrah on the hamzah in **(idbar al-nujum)**, the Seven [Readers] recited it as a verbal noun (*masdar*), according to what we explained in Surat Qaf. Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayt'a recited **(wa-adbar)** with a fatha; the same was reported from Ya'qub, Sallam, and Ayyub. It is the plural of *dubr* and *dubur*, and *dubr al-amr* and *duburuhu* means its end.

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from the hadith of Muhammad ibn Fudayl, from Rishdin ibn Kurayb, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, from the Prophet ﷺ who said: "*Idbar al-nujum* is the two rak'ahs before dawn, and *idbar al-sujud* is the two rak'ahs after Maghrib." He said: a gharib hadith; we do not know it as marfu' except through this chain, from the hadith of Muhammad ibn Fudayl from Rishdin ibn Kurayb. I asked Muhammad ibn Isma'il about Muhammad ibn Fudayl and Rishdin ibn Kurayb, which of them is more reliable? He said: they are close, and Muhammad is more preponderant in my view. He said: I also asked Abdullah ibn Abd al-Rahman about this, and he said: they are close, and Rishdin ibn Kurayb is more preponderant in my view. Al-Tirmidhi said: what Abu Muhammad said is correct, and Rishdin ibn Kurayb is more preponderant in my view than Muhammad and earlier, for Rishdin met Ibn Abbas and saw him.

In Sahih Muslim, it is reported from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ was not more persistent in any voluntary prayer than in the two rak'ahs before dawn." [[In N: "more persistent in the two rak'ahs of dawn before the morning prayer."]] And from her, from the Prophet ﷺ who said: "The two rak'ahs of dawn are better than the world and all it contains."

Here ends the tafsir (exegesis) of Surat al-Tur, and praise be to Allah.
